report:
I have enough evidence now to write a balanced conclusion.

## Conclusion

The evidence is genuinely mixed, but on balance it supports skepticism about a meaningful clinical benefit—so your "no" leans toward being reasonably well-supported, especially for larger, higher-quality trials.

**Early evidence suggested benefit.** Older Cochrane reviews (pre-2020) and pediatric meta-analyses concluded probiotics "shorten the duration and reduce stool frequency" in acute infectious diarrhea, based on pooled small trials (Cochrane Library, https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD003048.pub3/abstract).

**However, the updated, more rigorous 2020 Cochrane review reversed this confidence.** After applying GRADE certainty assessments, the authors concluded that "probiotics may not affect how long acute diarrhoea lasts" and that "we do not know if they can shorten the time to recovery," citing low-to-very-low certainty evidence, heterogeneity across probiotic strains/doses, and risk of bias in included trials (PMC, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8166250/).

**The strongest recent evidence—two large, well-designed multicenter RCTs published in NEJM (2018)—found no significant benefit.** Schnadower et al. (PECARN, U.S. emergency departments) and a companion Canadian trial by Freedman et al. both tested common probiotic formulations (including Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG) in children with acute gastroenteritis and found no meaningful reduction in diarrhea duration or severity compared to placebo (NPR summary, https://www.npr.org/sections/health-shots/2018/11/21/669373363/probiotics-found-to-be-ineffective-for-easing-symptoms-of-kids-stomach-bugs; NYT, https://www.nytimes.com/2018/11/26/well/eat/probiotics-do-not-ease-stomach-flu.html).

**Bottom line:** Earlier positive findings largely came from smaller, heterogeneous, lower-quality trials. When evidence certainty is rigorously assessed and large well-powered trials are considered, benefit is inconsistent or absent—particularly in children in developed-country settings, which is where the best trials have been conducted. Effects, if any, appear strain-specific and modest at best, not a general "probiotics work" conclusion.
